newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets pause for breath after dizzying rise.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets pause for breath after dizzying rise.

text.p: World oil markets traded quietly on Tuesday, pausing to recover breath after a dizzying near $2 rise over the past five days.
Benchmark Brent crude oil futures slipped back slightly in London morning trade as dealers took profits after yesterday's 77 cent rally, which pushed oil prices to a two-month high.
But by 1430 gmt the June contract was only two cents down at $19.70 a barrel, while in New York June crude futures were off by the same amount at $21.36.
Dealers in New York and London described it as a day of consolidation as oil refinery buyers came to terms with the sharp fall in profitability that crude's rise has inflicted on their operations.

Crude sellers were relaxed as they assessed the durability of the market rally, which has defied predictions of a price slump predicated on estimates that galloping oil production will outstrip stagnating demand.

Dealers said the market continued to ignore bearish fundamentals and derive mild support from short-term supply problems, such as a U.S. refinery fire and renewed tribal unrest in the Nigerian oil fields.

An overnight blast and fire at Citgo Petroleum Corp's 135,000 barrel per day (bpd) refinery in Corpus Christi, Texas may tighten gasoline supplies at a time of increased U.S. demand ahead of summer peak driving season.
But traders said there had been little major effect on the gasoline market, which is well supplied with thousands of barrels soaked up from producers in Europe.
More significantly, the Royal Dutch Shell Group said tribal unrest in Nigeria had once again forced it to shut down facilities, cutting oil output by more than 10 percent.
Armed youths forced Shell to close five flow stations in the Nembe creek field as part of a dispute over relief material. The same facilities were blocked by violent tribal protests in March.
But the oil giant, which produces more than half of Nigeria's total output of two million barrels a day, said crude oil exports had not yet been affected.

In northern Scotland worries that a fishermen's blockade of Sullom Voe oil terminal would hinder liftings of benchmark North Sea Brent crude eased after threats of legal action forced the 14 small boats to end their action.
The fishermen were protesting against the alleged failure to pay them compensation for the damage done to their fishing grounds by the 1993 Braer oil spill.
Crude's rally was sparked last week by rumours oil field maintenance would cut deeply into the June North Sea export programme, tightening supplies.
Oil traders said they were now looking ahead to U.S. weekly supply and demand data, due for release later tonight, for the next clue to where crude prices will head.
European Union figures released on Tuesday showing a month on month rise in crude oil stocks of 3.1 percent last month, failed to dent the market's enthusiasm for higher prices.
